what_its_for: Enfortumab vedotin is a cancer medicine used to treat adults with a type of bladder or urinary tract cancer called urothelial cancer. It is used when other treatments, such as chemotherapy or immunotherapy, have not worked or are no longer working. It can also be used in combination with another medicine called pembrolizumab as a first treatment for certain patients with advanced urothelial cancer.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into a vein through a needle or catheter. You will receive this treatment at a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. You do not take this medicine at home on your own. Each infusion usually takes about 30 minutes. Your care team will watch you closely during and after each infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight (in kilograms). The typical dose is 1.25 mg per kilogram of body weight. It is given on Days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day treatment cycle, which means you receive it three times during each cycle with one week off at the end. Your doctor may adjust your dose or delay treatment if you experience side effects.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider, missing a dose is uncommon. However, if you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, contact your doctor or care team as soon as possible to arrange a new appointment. Do not try to make up a missed dose on your own. Your doctor will decide the best plan for getting back on your treatment schedule.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by trained healthcare professionals at the infusion center or pharmacy. You do not need to store it at home. If you are ever given information about at-home storage, keep it in a refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C), protect it from light, and do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, drowsy, or have vision changes. Avoid spending too much time in the sun and use sunscreen and protective clothing, as this medicine can make your skin very sensitive to sunlight. Avoid starting new medicines, herbal supplements, or vitamins without first talking to your doctor, since some may interfere with how this medicine works. Women who could become pregnant and men with female partners of childbearing age should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: a serious skin rash, blistering, or peeling of the skin (these could be signs of a dangerous skin condition); numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hands or feet (nerve damage); severe eye irritation, dry eyes, or vision changes; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurred vision; signs of a serious lung problem such as new or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain; fever, chills, or other signs of infection; severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach pain; unusual tiredness or weakness; or any swelling, redness, or pain at the IV site during your infusion.
when_it_works: Your doctor will check how well the medicine is working through regular tests, scans, and appointments. Some patients may notice improvements within the first few months of treatment, but every person is different. It is important to keep all of your scheduled appointments so your care team can monitor your response to treatment and manage any side effects.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Women who are pregnant should not use this medicine. Women who could become pregnant and men with female partners who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose. Liver Problems: If you have moderate or severe liver problems, your doctor may adjust your dose or may decide this medicine is not right for you. Always tell your doctor about all of your health conditions before starting treatment. Older Adults: This medicine has been used in older adults, but older patients may be more sensitive to certain side effects such as nerve damage or skin reactions. Your care team will monitor you closely.
